senses.d: I, the ninth letter of the English alphabet, takes its form from the Phœnician, through the Latin and the Greek. The Phœnician letter was probably of Egyptian origin. Its original value was nearly the same as that of the Italian I, or long e as in mete. Etymologically I is most closely related to e, y, j, g; as in dint, dent, beverage, L. bibere; E. kin, AS. cynn; E. thin, AS. þynne; E. dominion, donjon, dungeon.
In our old authors, I was often used for ay (or aye), yes, which is pronounced nearly like it.
As a numeral, I stands for 1, II for 2, etc.
The nominative case of the pronoun of the first person; the word with which a speaker or writer denotes himself.

I.etym: [OE. i, ich, ic, AS. ic; akin to OS. & D. ik, OHG. ih, G. ich, Icel. ek, Dan. jeg, Sw. jag, Goth. ik, OSlav. az', Russ. ia, W. i, L. ego, Gr. εγὤ, εγὤν, Skr. aham. √179. Cf. Egoism.]

senses.d: Water or other fluid frozen or reduced to the solid state by cold; frozen water. It is a white or transparent colorless substance, crystalline, brittle, and viscoidal. Its specific gravity (0.92, that of water at 4° C. being 1.0) being less than that of water, ice floats.
Concreted sugar.
Water, cream, custard, etc., sweetened, flavored, and artificially frozen.
Any substance having the appearance of ice; as, camphor ice.

Ice.etym: [OE. is, iis, AS. īs; aksin to D. ijs, G. eis, OHG. īs, Icel. īss, Sw. is, Dan. iis, and perh. to E. iron.]

senses.d: To cover with ice; to convert into ice, or into something resembling ice.
To cover with icing, or frosting made of sugar and milk or white of egg; to frost, as cakes, tarts, etc.
To chill or cool, as with ice; to freeze.
Of no account; useless; vain; trifling; unprofitable; thoughtless; silly; barren.
q: Every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.
Down their idle weapons dropped.
This idle story became important.

senses.d: Not called into active service; not turned to appropriate use; unemployed; as, idle hours.
q: The idle spear and shield were high uphing.

senses.d: Not employed; unoccupied with business; inactive; doing nothing; as, idle workmen.
q: Why stand ye here all the day idle?

senses.d: Given rest and ease; averse to labor or employment; lazy; slothful; as, an idle fellow.
Light-headed; foolish.

Idle.syn: Unoccupied; unemployed; vacant; inactive; indolent; sluggish; slothful; useless; ineffectual; futile; frivolous; vain; trifling; unprofitable; unimportant.
Idle.etym: [OE. idel, AS. īdel vain, empty, useless; akin to OS. īdal, D. ijdel, OHG. ītal vain, empty, mere, G. eitel, Dan. & Sw. idel mere, pure, and prob. to Gr. � clear, pure, � to burn. Cf. Ether.]

senses.d: To lose or spend time in inaction, or without being employed in business.
To spend in idleness; to waste; to consume; — often followed by away; as, to idle away an hour a day.
The condition or quality of being idle (in the various senses of that word); uselessness; fruitlessness; triviality; inactivity; laziness.
An image or representation of anything.
q: Do her adore with sacred reverence, As th' idol of her maker's great magnificence.

senses.d: An image of a divinity; a representation or symbol of a deity or any other being or thing, made or used as an object of worship; a similitude of a false god.
q: That they should not worship devils, and idols of gold.

senses.d: That on which the affections are strongly (often excessively) set; an object of passionate devotion; a person or thing greatly loved or adored.
q: The soldier's god and people's idol.

senses.d: A false notion or conception; a fallacy.
q: The idols of preconceived opinion.

Idol.etym: [OE. idole, F. idole, L. idolum, fr. Gr. �, fr. � that which is seen, the form, shape, figure, fr. � to see. See Wit, and cf. Eidolon.]

senses.d: A worshiper of idols; one who pays divine honors to images, statues, or representations of anything made by hands; one who worships as a deity that which is not God; a pagan.
An adorer; a great admirer.
q: Jonson was an idolater of the ancients.

Idolater.etym: [F. idolâtre: cf. L. idololatres, Gr. �. See Idolatry.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to idolatry; partaking of the nature of idolatry; given to idolatry or the worship of false gods; as, idolatrous sacrifices.
q: put down the idolatrous priests.

senses.d: Consisting in, or partaking of, an excessive attachment or reverence; as, an idolatrous veneration for antiquity.
The worship of idols, images, or anything which is not God; the worship of false gods.
q: His eye surveyed the dark idolatries Of alienated Judah.

senses.d: Excessive attachment or veneration for anything; respect or love which borders on adoration.

Idolatry.etym: [F. idolâtrie, LL. idolatria, L. idololatria, Fr. Gr. �; � idol + � service.]

senses.d: In case that; granting, allowing, or supposing that; — introducing a condition or supposition.
q: Tisiphone, that oft hast heard my prayer, Assist, if Œdipus deserve thy care.
If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread.

senses.d: Whether; — in dependent questions.
q: Uncertain if by augury or chance.
She doubts if two and two make four.

If.etym: [OE. if, gif, AS. gif; akin to OFries. ief, gef, ef, OS. ef, of, D. of, or, whether, if, G. ob whether, if, OHG. oba, ibu, Icel. ef, Goth. iba, ibai, an interrogative particle; properly a case form of a noun meaning, doubt (cf. OHG. iba doubt, condition, Icel. if, ef, ifi, efi), and therefore orig.

senses.d: Public disgrace or dishonor; reproach; infamy.
q: Their generals have been received with honor after their defeat; yours with ignominy after conquest.
Vice begins in mistake, and ends in ignominy.
Ignominy is the infliction of such evil as is made dishonorable, or the deprivation of such good as is made honorable by the Commonwealth.

senses.d: An act deserving disgrace; an infamous act.

Ignominy.etym: [L. ignominia ignominy (i.e., a deprivation of one's good name); in- not + nomen name: cf. F. ignominie. See In- not, and Name.]

senses.d: The condition of being ignorant; the want of knowledge in general, or in relation to a particular subject; the state of being uneducated or uninformed.
q: Ignorance is the curse of God, Knowledge the wing wherewith we fly to heaven.

senses.d: A willful neglect or refusal to acquire knowledge which one may acquire and it is his duty to have.
Destitute of knowledge; uninstructed or uninformed; untaught; unenlightened.
q: He that doth not know those things which are of use for him to know, is but an ignorant man, whatever he may know besides.

senses.d: Unacquainted with; unconscious or unaware; — used with of.
q: Ignorant of guilt, I fear not shame.

senses.d: Unknown; undiscovered.
q: Ignorant concealment.
Alas, what ignorant sin have I committed?

senses.d: Resulting from ignorance; foolish; silly.
q: His shipping, Poor ignorant baubles! — on our terrible seas, Like eggshells moved.
In such business Action is eloquence, and the eyes of the ignorant More learned than the ears.
In the first ages of Christianity, not only the learned and the wise, but the ignorant and illiterate, embraced torments and death.

Ignorant.syn: Uninstructed; untaught; unenlightened; uninformed; unlearned; unlettered; illiterate. — Ignorant, Illiterate. Ignorant denotes want of knowledge, either as to single subject or information in general; illiterate refers to an ignorance of letters, or of knowledge acquired by reading and study. In the Middle Ages, a great proportion of the higher classes were illiterate, and yet were far from being ignorant, especially in regard to war and other active pursuits.
Ignorant.etym: [F., fr. L. ignorans, -antis, p. pr. of ignorare to be ignorant. See Ignore.]

senses.d: A person untaught or uninformed; one unlettered or unskilled; an ignoramous.
q: Did I for this take pains to teach Our zealous ignorants to preach?

senses.d: In a ignorant manner; without knowledge; inadvertently.
q: Whom therefoer ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you.

senses.d: Contrary to good, in a physical sense; contrary or opposed to advantage, happiness, etc.; bad; evil; unfortunate; disagreeable; unfavorable.
q: Neither is it ill air only that maketh an ill seat, but ill ways, ill markets, and ill neighbors.
There 's some ill planet reigns.

senses.d: Contrary to good, in a moral sense; evil; wicked; wrong; iniquitious; naughtly; bad; improper.
q: Of his own body he was ill, and gave The clergy ill example.

senses.d: Sick; indisposed; unwell; diseased; disordered; as, ill of a fever.
q: I am in health, I breathe, and see thee ill.

senses.d: Not according with rule, fitness, or propriety; incorrect; rude; unpolished; inelegant.
q: That 's an ill phrase.

Ill.syn: Bad; evil; wrong; wicked; sick; unwell.
Ill.etym: [OE. ill, ille, Icel. illr; akin to Sw. illa, adv., Dan. ilde, adv.]

senses.d: Whatever annoys or impairs happiness, or prevents success; evil of any kind; misfortune; calamity; disease; pain; as, the ills of humanity.
q: Who can all sense of others' ills escape Is but a brute at best in human shape.
That makes us rather bear those ills we have Than fly to others that we know not of.

senses.d: Whatever is contrary to good, in a moral sense; wickedness; depravity; iniquity; wrong; evil.
q: Strong virtue, like strong nature, struggles still, Exerts itself, and then throws off the ill.

senses.d: In a ill manner; badly; weakly.
q: How ill this taper burns!
Ill fares the land, to hastening ills a prey, Where wealth accumulates and men decay.

senses.d: To make light; to throw light on; to supply with light, literally or figuratively; to brighten.
To light up; to decorate with artificial lights, as a building or city, in token of rejoicing or respect.
To adorn, as a book or page with borders, initial letters, or miniature pictures in colors and gold, as was done in manuscripts of the Middle Ages.
To make plain or clear; to dispel the obscurity to by knowledge or reason; to explain; to elucidate; as, to illuminate a text, a problem, or a duty.

Illuminate.etym: [L. illuminatus, p. p. of illuminare; pref. il- in + luminare to enlighten, fr. lumen light. See Luminous, and cf. Illume, Illumine, Enlimn, Limn.]

senses.d: To light up in token or rejoicing.
Enlightened.
One who is enlightened; esp., a pretender to extraordinary light and knowledge.

An imitation, representation, or similitude of any person, thing, or act, sculptured, drawn, painted, or otherwise made perceptible to the sight; a visible presentation; a copy; a likeness; an effigy; a picture; a semblance.
q: Even like a stony image, cold and numb.
Whose is this image and superscription?
This play is the image of a murder done in Vienna.
And God created man in his own image.

senses.d: Hence: The likeness of anything to which worship is paid; an idol.
q: Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, . . . thou shalt not bow down thyself to them.

senses.d: Show; appearance; cast.
q: The face of things a frightful image bears.

senses.d: A representation of anything to the mind; a picture drawn by the fancy; a conception; an idea.
q: Can we conceive Image of aught delightful, soft, or great?

senses.d: A picture, example, or illustration, often taken from sensible objects, and used to illustrate a subject; usually, an extended metaphor.

The figure or picture of any object formed at the focus of a lens or mirror, by rays of light from the several points of the object symmetrically refracted or reflected to corresponding points in such focus; this may be received on a screen, a photographic plate, or the retina of the eye, and viewed directly by the eye, or with an eyeglass, as in the telescope and microscope; the likeness of an object formed by reflection; as, to see one's image in a mirror.

Image.etym: [F., fr. L. imago, imaginis, from the root of imitari to imitate. See Imitate, and cf. Imagine.]

senses.d: To represent or form an image of; as, the still lake imaged the shore; the mirror imaged her figure.
To represent to the mental vision; to form a likeness of by the fancy or recollection; to imagine.
q: Condemn'd whole years in absence to deplore, And image charms he must behold no more.

senses.d: The work of one who makes images or visible representation of objects; imitation work; images in general, or in mass.
q: In those oratories might you see Rich carvings, portraitures, and imagery.

senses.d: Fig.: Unreal show; imitation; appearance.
q: What can thy imagery of sorrow mean?

senses.d: The work of the imagination or fancy; false ideas; imaginary phantasms.
q: The imagery of a melancholic fancy.

senses.d: Rhetorical decoration in writing or speaking; vivid descriptions presenting or suggesting images of sensible objects; figures in discourse.
q: I wish there may be in this poem any instance of good imagery.

senses.d: The imagine-making power of the mind; the power to create or reproduce ideally an object of sense previously perceived; the power to call up mental imagines.
q: Our simple apprehension of corporeal objects, if present, is sense; if absent, is imagination.
Imagination is of three kinds: joined with belief of that which is to come; joined with memory of that which is past; and of things present, or as if they were present.

senses.d: The representative power; the power to reconstruct or recombine the materials furnished by direct apprehension; the complex faculty usually termed the plastic or creative power; the fancy.
q: The imagination of common language — the productive imagination of philosophers — is nothing but the representative process plus the process to which I would give the name of the “comparative.”
The power of the mind to decompose its conceptions, and to recombine the elements of them at its pleasure, is called its faculty of imagination.

The business of conception is to present us with an exact transcript of what we have felt or perceived. But we have moreover a power of modifying our conceptions, by combining the parts of different ones together, so as to form new wholes of our creation. I shall employ the word imagination to express this power.

senses.d: The power to recombine the materials furnished by experience or memory, for the accomplishment of an elevated purpose; the power of conceiving and expressing the ideal.
q: The lunatic, the lover, and the poet Are of imagination all compact . . . The poet's eye, in a fine frenzy rolling, Doth glance from heaven to earth, from earth to heaven, And as imagination bodies forth The forms of things unknown, the poet's pen Turns them to shapes, and gives to airy nothing A local habitation and a name.

senses.d: A mental image formed by the action of the imagination as a faculty; a conception; a notion.
q: The same power, which we should call fancy if employed on a production of a light nature, would be dignified with the title of imagination if shown on a grander scale.

Imagination.syn: Conception; idea; conceit; fancy; device; origination; invention; scheme; design; purpose; contrivance.
Imagination.etym: [OE. imaginacionum, F. imagination, fr. L. imaginatio. See Imagine.]

senses.d: To form in the mind a notion or idea of; to form a mental image of; to conceive; to produce by the imagination.
q: In the night, imagining some fear, How easy is a bush supposed a bear!

senses.d: To contrive in purpose; to scheme; to devise; to compass; to purpose. See Compass, v. t., 5.
q: How long will ye imagine mischief against a man?

senses.d: To represent to one's self; to think; to believe.

Imagine.syn: To fancy; conceive; apprehend; think; believe; suppose; opine; deem; plan; scheme; devise.
Imagine.etym: [F. imaginer, L. imaginari, p. p. imaginatus, fr. imago image. See Image.]

senses.d: To form images or conceptions; to conceive; to devise.
To think; to suppose.
q: My sister is not so defenseless left As you imagine.

senses.d: God with us; — an appellation of the Christ.

Immanuel.etym: [Heb. 'immān�ēl, fr. 'im with + ān� us + ēl God.]

senses.d: Not separated in respect to place by anything intervening; proximate; close; as, immediate contact.
q: You are the most immediate to our throne.

senses.d: Not deferred by an interval of time; present; instant.
q: Death . . . not yet inflicted, as he feared, By some immediate stroke.

senses.d: Acting with nothing interposed or between, or without the intervention of another object as a cause, means, or agency; acting, perceived, or produced, directly; as, an immediate cause.
q: The immediate knowledge of the past is therefore impossible.

Immediate.etym: [F. immédiat. See In- not, and Mediate.]

senses.d: In an immediate manner; without intervention of any other person or thing; proximately; directly; — opposed to mediately; as, immediately contiguous.
q: God's acceptance of it either immediately by himself, or mediately by the hands of the bishop.

senses.d: Without interval of time; without delay; promptly; instantly; at once.
q: And Jesus . . . touched him, saying, I will; be thou clean. And immediately his leprosy was cleansed.

senses.d: As soon as. Cf. Directly, 8, Note.

Immediately.syn: Directly; instantly; quickly; forthwith; straightway; presently. See Directly.

senses.d: Not mortal; exempt from liability to die; undying; imperishable; lasting forever; having unlimited, or eternal, existance.
q: Unto the King eternal, immortal, invisible.
For my soul, what can it do to that, Being a thing immortal as itself?

senses.d: Connected with, or pertaining to immortality.
q: I have immortal longings in me.

senses.d: Destined to live in all ages of this world; abiding; exempt from oblivion; imperishable; as, immortal fame.
q: One of the few, immortal names, That were not born to die.

senses.d: Great; excessive; grievous.

Immortal.syn: Eternal; everlasting; never-ending; ceaseless; perpetual; continual; enduring; endless; imperishable; incorruptible; deathless; undying.
Immortal.etym: [L. immortalis; pref. im- not + mortalis mortal: cf. F. immortel. See Mortal, and cf. Immortelle.]

senses.d: One who will never cease to be; one exempt from death, decay, or annihilation.
The quality or state of being immortal; exemption from death and annihilation; unending existance; as, the immortality of the soul.
q: This mortal must put on immortality.

senses.d: Exemption from oblivion; perpetuity; as, the immortality of fame.
The state or quality of being immutable; immutableness.
Not mutable; not capable or susceptible of change; unchangeable; unalterable.
q: That by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation.
Immutable, immortal, infinite, Eternal King.

Immutable.etym: [L. immutabilis; pref. im- not + mutabilis mutable. See Mutable.]

senses.d: To bestow a share or portion of; to give, grant, or communicate; to allow another to partake in; as, to impart food to the poor; the sun imparts warmth.
q: Well may he then to you his cares impart.

senses.d: To obtain a share of; to partake of.
To communicate the knowledge of; to make known; to show by words or tokens; to tell; to disclose.
q: Gentle lady, When I did first impart my love to you.

Impart.syn: To share; yield; confer; convey; grant; give; reveal; disclose; discover; divulge. See Communicate.
Impart.etym: [OF. impartir, empartir, L. impartire, impertire; pref. im- in + partire to part, divide, fr. pars, partis, part, share. See Part, n. ]

senses.d: To give a part or share.
q: He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none.

senses.d: To hold a conference or consultation.
That which impedes or hinders progress, motion, activity, or effect.
q: Thus far into the bowels of the land Have we marched on without impediment.
The eloquence of Demosthenes was to Philip of Macedon, a difficulty to be met with his best resources, an obstacle to his own ambition, and an impediment in his political career.

senses.d: To impede.
Not penitent; not repenting of sin; not contrite; of a hard heart.

Impenitent.etym: [L. impaenitens; pref. im- not + paenitens penitens: cf. F. impénitent. See Penitent.]

senses.d: One who is not penitent.
Commanding; ascendant; imperial; lordly; majestic.
q: Therefore, great lords, be, as your titles witness, Imperious.

senses.d: Haughly; arrogant; overbearing; as, an imperious tyrant; an imperious manner.
q: This imperious man will work us all From princes into pages.
His bold, contemptuous, and imperious spirit soon made him conspicuous.

senses.d: Imperative; urgent; compelling.
q: Imperious need, which can not be withstood.

Imperious.syn: Dictatorial; haughty; domineering; overbearing; lordly; tyrannical; despotic; arrogant; imperative; authoritative; commanding; pressing.
Imperious.etym: [L. imperiosus: cf. F. impérieux. See Imperial.]

senses.d: Not placable; not to be appeased; incapable of being pacified; inexorable; as, an implacable prince.
q: I see thou art implacable.
An object of implacable enmity.

senses.d: Incapable of being relieved or assuaged; inextinguishable.
q: O! how I burn with implacable fire.
Which wrought them pain Implacable, and many a dolorous groan.

Implacable.syn: Unappeasable; inexorable; irreconcilable; unrelenting; relentless; unyielding.
Implacable.etym: [L. implacabilis; pref. im- not + placabilis: cf. F. implacable. See Placable.]

senses.d: To institute and prosecute a suit against, in court; to sue or prosecute at law; hence, to accuse; to impeach.
To sue at law.
The quality of being importunate; pressing or pertinacious solicitation; urgent request; incessant or frequent application; troublesome pertinacity.
q: O'ercome with importunity and tears.

Importunity.etym: [L. importunitas unsuitableness, rudeness: cf. F. importunité.]

senses.d: To lay on; to set or place; to put; to deposit.
q: Cakes of salt and barley did impose Within a wicker basket.

senses.d: To lay as a charge, burden, tax, duty, obligation, command, penalty, etc.; to enjoin; to levy; to inflict; as, to impose a toll or tribute.
q: What fates impose, that men must needs abide.
Death is the penalty imposed.
Thou on the deep imposest nobler laws.

senses.d: To lay on, as the hands, in the religious rites of confirmation and ordination.
To arrange in proper order on a table of stone or metal and lock up in a chase for printing; — said of columns or pages of type, forms, etc.

Impose.etym: [F. imposer; pref. im- in + poser to place. See Pose, v. t.]

senses.d: To practice tricks or deception.
A command; injunction.

Not possible; incapable of being done, of existing, etc.; unattainable in the nature of things, or by means at command; insuperably difficult under the circumstances; absurd or impracticable; not feasible.
q: With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible.
Without faith it is impossible to please him.

Impossible.etym: [F., fr. L. impossibilis; pref. im- not + possibilis possible. See Possible.]

senses.d: An impossibility.
q: “Madam,” quoth he, “this were an impossible!”

senses.d: Not potent; wanting power, strength. or vigor. whether physical, intellectual, or moral; deficient in capacity; destitute of force; weak; feeble; infirm.
q: There sat a certain man at Lystra, impotent inhis feet.
O most lame and impotent conclusion!
Not slow to hear, Nor impotent to save.

senses.d: Wanting the power of self-restraint; incontrolled; ungovernable; violent.
q: Impotent of tongue, her silence broke.

senses.d: Wanting the power of procreation; unable to copulate; also, sometimes, sterile; barren.

Impotent.etym: [F. impotent, L. impotens, -entis; pref. im- not + potens potent, powerful. See Potent.]

senses.d: One who is impotent.
To make poor; to reduce to poverty or indigence; as, misfortune and disease impoverish families.
To exhaust the strength, richness, or fertility of; to make sterile; as, to impoverish land.

Impoverish.etym: [OF. empovrir; pref. em- (L. in) + povre poor, F. pauvre; cf. OF. apovrir, F. appauvrir, where the prefix is a-, L. ad. Cf. Empoverish, and see Poor, and -ish.]

senses.d: To put in prison or jail; To arrest and detain in custody; to confine.
q: He imprisoned was in chains remediless.

senses.d: To limit, restrain, or confine in any way.
q: Try to imprison the resistless wind.

Imprison.etym: [OE. enprisonen, OF. enprisoner, F. emprisonner; pref. en- (L. in) + F. & OF. prison. See Prison.]

senses.d: The act of imprisoning, or the state of being imprisoned; confinement; restraint.
q: His sinews waxen weak and raw Through long imprisonment and hard constraint.
Every confinement of the person is an imprisonment, whether it be in a common prison, or in a private house, or even by foreibly detaining one in the public streets.

senses.d: Bold, with contempt or disregard; unblushingly forward; impertinent; wanting modesty; shameless; saucy.
q: More than impudent sauciness.
When we behold an angel, not to fear Is to be impudent.

Impudent.syn: Shameless; audacious; brazen; bold-faced; pert; immodest; rude; saucy; impertinent; insolent.
Impudent.etym: [L. impudens, -entis; pref. im- not + pudens ashamed, modest, p. pr. of pudere to feel shame: cf. F. impudent.]

senses.d: To charge; to ascribe; to attribute; to set to the account of; to charge to one as the author, responsible originator, or possessor; — generally in a bad sense.
q: Nor you, ye proud, impute to these the fault, If memory o'er their tomb no trophies raise.
One vice of a darker shade was imputed to him — envy.

senses.d: To adjudge as one's own (the sin or righteousness) of another; as, the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us.
q: It was imputed to him for righteousness.
They merit Imputed shall absolve them who renounce Their own, both righteous and unrighteous deeds.

senses.d: To take account of; to consider; to regard.
q: If we impute this last humiliation as the cause of his death.

Impute.syn: To ascribe; attribute; charge; reckon; consider; imply; insinuate; refer. See Ascribe.
Impute.etym: [F. imputer, L. imputare to bring into the reckoning, charge, impute; pref. im- in + putare to reckon, think. See Putative.]

senses.d: The specific signification of in is situation or place with respect to surrounding, environment, encompassment, etc. It is used with verbs signifying being, resting, or moving within limits, or within circumstances or conditions of any kind conceived of as limiting, confining, or investing, either wholly or in part. In its different applications, it approaches some of the meanings of, and sometimes is interchangeable with, within, into, on, at, of, and among.
With reference to space or place; as, he lives in Boston; he traveled in Italy; castles in the air.
q: The babe lying in a manger.
Thy sun sets weeping in the lowly west.
Situated in the forty-first degree of latitude.
Matter for censure in every page.

senses.d: With reference to circumstances or conditions; as, he is in difficulties; she stood in a blaze of light.
q: Wrapt in sweet sounds, as in bright veils.

senses.d: With reference to a whole which includes or comprises the part spoken of; as, the first in his family; the first regiment in the army.
q: Nine in ten of those who enter the ministry.

senses.d: With reference to physical surrounding, personal states, etc., abstractly denoted; as, I am in doubt; the room is in darkness; to live in fear.
q: When shall we three meet again, In thunder, lightning, or in rain?

senses.d: With reference to character, reach, scope, or influence considered as establishing a limitation; as, to be in one's favor.
q: Sounds inharmonious in themselves, and harsh.

senses.d: With reference to movement or tendency toward a certain limit or environment; — sometimes equivalent to into; as, to put seed in the ground; to fall in love; to end in death; to put our trust in God.
q: He would not plunge his brother in despair.
She had no jewels to deposit in their caskets.

senses.d: With reference to a limit of time; as, in an hour; it happened in the last century; in all my life.

In.syn: Into; within; on; at. See At.
In.etym: [AS. in; akin to D. & G. in, Icel. ī, Sw. & Dan. i, OIr. & L. in, Gr. εν̓. √197. Cf. 1st In-, Inn.]

senses.d: Not out; within; inside. In, the preposition, becomes an adverb by omission of its object, leaving it as the representative of an adverbial phrase, the context indicating what the omitted object is; as, he takes in the situation (i.e., he comprehends it in his mind); the Republicans were in (i.e., in office); in at one ear and out at the other (i.e., in or into the head); his side was in (i.e., in the turn at the bat); he came in (i.e., into the house).
q: Their vacation . . . falls in so pat with ours.

senses.d: With privilege or possession; — used to denote a holding, possession, or seisin; as, in by descent; in by purchase; in of the seisin of her husband.
One who is in office; — the opposite of out.
A reëntrant angle; a nook or corner.
q: All the ins and outs of this neighborhood.

senses.d: To inclose; to take in; to harvest.
q: He that ears my land spares my team and gives me leave to in the crop.

senses.d: In like degree; in like manner; seeing that; considering that; since; — followed by as. See In as much as, under In, prep.
q: Inasmuch as ye did it not to one of the least of these, ye did it not to me.

Inasmuch.syn: Because; since; for; as. See Because.

senses.d: To set on fire; to inflame; to kindle; to burn.
q: Twelve Trojan princes wait on thee, and labor to incense Thy glorious heap of funeral.

senses.d: To inflame with anger; to endkindle; to fire; to incite; to provoke; to heat; to madden.
q: The people are incensed him.

Incense.syn: To enrage; exasperate; provoke; anger; irritate; heat; fire; instigate.
Incense.etym: [L. incensus, p. p. of incendere; pref. in- in + root of candere to glow. See Candle.]

senses.d: To offer incense to. See Incense.
To perfume with, or as with, incense.

Incense.etym: [LL. incensare: cf. F. encenser. See Incense, n.]

senses.d: The perfume or odors exhaled from spices and gums when burned in celebrating religious rites or as an offering to some deity.
q: A thick cloud of incense went up.

senses.d: The materials used for the purpose of producing a perfume when burned, as fragrant gums, spices, frankincense, etc.
q: Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, took either of them his censer, and put fire therein, and put incense thereon.

senses.d: Also used figuratively.
q: Or heap the shrine of luxury and pride, With incense kindled at the Muse's flame.

Incense.etym: [OE. encens, F. encens, L. incensum, fr. incensus, p. p. of incendere to burn. See Incense to inflame.]

senses.d: Angered; enraged.
Represented as enraged, as any wild creature depicted with fire issuing from mouth and eyes.
To deviate from a line, direction, or course, toward an object; to lean; to tend; as, converging lines incline toward each other; a road inclines to the north or south.
Fig.: To lean or tend, in an intellectual or moral sense; to favor an opinion, a course of conduct, or a person; to have a propensity or inclination; to be disposed.
q: Their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech.
Power finds its balance, giddy motions cease In both the scales, and each inclines to peace.

senses.d: To bow; to incline the head.

Incline.syn: To lean; slope; slant; tend; bend.
Incline.etym: [OE. inclinen, enclinen, OF. encliner, incliner, F. incliner, L. inclinare; pref. in- in + clinare to bend, incline; akin to E. lean. See Lean to incline.]

senses.d: To cause to deviate from a line, position, or direction; to give a leaning, bend, or slope to; as, incline the column or post to the east; incline your head to the right.
q: Incline thine ear, O Lord, and hear.

senses.d: To impart a tendency or propensity to, as to the will or affections; to turn; to dispose; to influence.
q: Incline my heart unto thy testimonies.
Incline our hearts to keep this law.

senses.d: To bend; to cause to stoop or bow; as, to incline the head or the body in acts of reverence or civility.
q: With due respect my body I inclined.

senses.d: An inclined plane; an ascent or descent; a grade or gradient; a slope.
Having a leaning or tendency towards, or away from, a thing; disposed or moved by wish, desire, or judgment; as, a man inclined to virtue.
Making an angle with some line or plane; — said of a line or plane.
Bent out of a perpendicular position, or into a curve with the convex side uppermost.
To surround; to shut in; to confine on all sides; to include; to shut up; to encompass; as, to inclose a fort or an army with troops; to inclose a town with walls.
q: How many evils have inclosed me round!

senses.d: To put within a case, envelope, or the like; to fold (a thing) within another or into the same parcel; as, to inclose a letter or a bank note.
q: The inclosed copies of the treaty.

senses.d: To separate from common grounds by a fence; as, to inclose lands.
To put into harness; to harness.
q: They went to coach and their horse inclose.

senses.d: Not continent; uncontrolled; not restraining the passions or appetites, particularly the sexual appetite; indulging unlawful lust; unchaste; lewd.
Unable to restrain natural evacuations.

Incontinent.etym: [L. incontinens: cf. F. incontinent. See In- not, and Continent.]

senses.d: One who is unchaste.
Incontinently; instantly; immediately.
q: He says he will return incontinent.

senses.d: Not corruptible; incapable of corruption, decay, or dissolution; as, gold is incorruptible.
q: Our bodies shall be changed into incorruptible and immortal substances.

senses.d: Incapable of being bribed or morally corrupted; inflexibly just and upright.

Incorruptible.etym: [L. incorruptibilis: cf. F. incorruptible. See In- not, and Corrupt.]

senses.d: One of a religious sect which arose in Alexandria, in the reign of the Emperor Justinian, and which believed that the body of Christ was incorruptible, and that he suffered hunger, thirst, pain, only in appearance.
The condition or quality of being incorrupt or incorruptible; absence of, or exemption from, corruption.
q: It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption.
The same preservation, or, rather, incorruption, we have observed in the flesh of turkeys, capons, etc.

Incorruption.etym: [L. incorruptio: cf. F. incorruption. See In- not, and Corruption.]

senses.d: To become greater or more in size, quantity, number, degree, value, intensity, power, authority, reputation, wealth; to grow; to augment; to advance; — opposed to decrease.
q: The waters increased and bare up the ark.
He must increase, but I must decrease.
The heavens forbid But that our loves and comforts should increase, Even as our days do grow!

senses.d: To multiply by the production of young; to be fertile, fruitful, or prolific.
q: Fishes are more numerous or increasing than beasts or birds, as appears by their numerous spawn.

senses.d: To become more nearly full; to show more of the surface; to wax; as, the moon increases.

Increase.syn: To enlarge; extend; multiply; expand; develop; heighten; amplify; raise; enhance; spread; aggravate; magnify; augment; advance.
Increase.etym: [OE. incresen, encresen, enrescen, OF. encreistre, fr. L. increscere; pref. in- in + crescere to grow. See Crescent, and cf. Decrease.]

senses.d: To augment or make greater in bulk, quantity, extent, value, or amount, etc.; to add to; to extend; to lengthen; to enhance; to aggravate; as, to increase one's possessions, influence.
q: I will increase the famine.
Make denials Increase your services.

senses.d: Addition or enlargement in size, extent, quantity, number, intensity, value, substance, etc.; augmentation; growth.
q: As if increase of appetite had grown By what it fed on.
For things of tender kind for pleasure made Shoot up with swift increase, and sudden are decay'd.

senses.d: That which is added to the original stock by augmentation or growth; produce; profit; interest.
q: Take thou no usury of him, or increase.
Let them not live to taste this land's increase.

senses.d: Progeny; issue; offspring.
q: All the increase of thy house shall die in the flower of their age.

senses.d: Generation.
The period of increasing light, or luminous phase; the waxing; — said of the moon.
q: Seeds, hair, nails, hedges, and herbs will grow soonest if set or cut in the increase of the moon.

Increase.syn: Enlargement; extension; growth; development; increment; addition; accession; production.
Increase.etym: [OE. encres, encresse. See Increase, v. i.]

senses.d: Not credible; surpassing belief; too extraordinary and improbable to admit of belief; unlikely; marvelous; fabulous.
q: Why should it be thought a thing incredible with you, that God should raise the dead?

Incredible.etym: [L. incredibilis: cf. OF. incredible. See In- not, and Credible.]

senses.d: Not capable of being cured; beyond the power of skill or medicine to remedy; as, an incurable disease.
q: A scirrhus is not absolutely incurable.

senses.d: Not admitting or capable of remedy or correction; irremediable; remediless; as, incurable evils.
q: Rancorous and incurable hostility.
They were laboring under a profound, and, as it might have seemed, an almost incurable ignorance.

Incurable.syn: Irremediable; remediless; irrecoverable; irretrievable; irreparable; hopeless.
Incurable.etym: [F. incurable, L. incurabilis. See In- not, and Curable.]

senses.d: A person diseased beyond cure.
Azure-colored; of a bright blue color.
To bring into debt; to place under obligation; — chiefly used in the participle indebted.
q: Thy fortune hath indebted thee to none.

Indebt.etym: [OE. endetten, F. endetter; pref. en- (L. in) + F. dette debt. See Debt.]

senses.d: Brought into debt; being under obligation; held to payment or requital; beholden.
q: By owing, owes not, but still pays, at once Indebted and discharged.

senses.d: Placed under obligation for something received, for which restitution or gratitude is due; as, we are indebted to our parents for their care of us in infancy; indebted to friends for help and encouragement.

In reality; in truth; in fact; verily; truly; — used in a variety of senses. Esp.: (a) Denoting emphasis; as, indeed it is so. (b) Denoting concession or admission; as, indeed, you are right. (c) Denoting surprise; as, indeed, is it you? Its meaning is not intrinsic or fixed, but depends largely on the form of expression which it accompanies.
q: The carnal mind is enmity against God; for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be.
I were a beast indeed to do you wrong.
There is, indeed, no great pleasure in visiting these magazines of war.

senses.d: A country in Southern Asia; the two peninsulas of Hither and Farther India; in a restricted sense, Hither India, or Hindostan.
The feeling excited by that which is unworthy, base, or disgraceful; anger mingled with contempt, disgust, or abhorrence.
q: Indignation expresses a strong and elevated disapprobation of mind, which is also inspired by something flagitious in the conduct of another.
When Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate, that he stood not up, nor moved for him, he was full of indignation against Mordecai.

senses.d: The effect of anger; punishment.
q: Hide thyself . . . until the indignation be overpast.

Indignation.syn: Anger; ire wrath; fury; rage. See Anger.

senses.d: To compose; to write; to be author of; to dictate; to prompt.
q: My heart is inditing a good matter.
Could a common grief have indited such expressions?
Hear how learned Greece her useful rules indites.

senses.d: To invite or ask.
q: She will indite him to some supper.

senses.d: To indict; to accuse; to censure.

Indite.etym: [OE. enditen to indite, indict, OF. enditer to indicate, show, dictate, write, inform, and endicter to accuse; both fr. LL. indictare to show, to accuse, fr. L. indicere to proclaim, announce; pref. in- in + dicere to say. The word was influenced also by L. indicare to indicate, and by dictare to di

senses.d: To compose; to write, as a poem.
q: Wounded I sing, tormented I indite.

senses.d: Given to industry; characterized by diligence; constantly, regularly, or habitually occupied; busy; assiduous; not slothful or idle; — commonly implying devotion to lawful and useful labor.
q: Frugal and industrious men are commonly friendly to the established government.

senses.d: Steadily and perseveringly active in a particular pursuit or aim; as, he was negligent in business, but industrious in pleasure; an industrious mischief maker.
q: Industrious to seek out the truth of all things.

Industrious.etym: [L. industrius, industriosus: cf. F. industrieux. See Industry.]

senses.d: Not excusable; not admitting excuse or justification; as, inexcusable folly.
q: Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest; for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things.

Inexcusable.etym: [L. inexcusabilis: cf. F. inexcusable. See Excuse.]

senses.d: Not fallible; not capable of erring; entirely exempt from liability to mistake; unerring; inerrable.
Not liable to fail, deceive, or disappoint; indubitable; sure; certain; as, infallible evidence; infallible success; an infallible remedy.
q: To whom also he showed himself alive, after his passion, by many infallible proofs.

senses.d: Incapable of error in defining doctrines touching faith or morals. See Papal infallibility, under Infallibility.

Infallible.etym: [Pref. in- not + fallible: cf. F. infallible.]

senses.d: Of very bad report; having a reputation of the worst kind; held in abhorrence; guilty of something that exposes to infamy; base; notoriously vile; detestable; as, an infamous traitor; an infamous perjurer.
q: False errant knight, infamous, and forsworn.

senses.d: Causing or producing infamy; deserving detestation; scandalous to the last degree; as, an infamous act; infamous vices; infamous corruption.
Branded with infamy by conviction of a crime; as, at common law, an infamous person can not be a witness.
Having a bad name as being the place where an odious crime was committed, or as being associated with something detestable; hence, unlucky; perilous; dangerous.
q: Infamous hills, and sandy perilous wilds.
The piny shade More infamous by cursed Lycaon made.

Infamous.syn: Detestable; odious; scandalous; disgraceful; base; vile; shameful; ignominious.
Infamous.etym: [Pref. in- not + famous: cf. L. infamis. See Infamy.]

senses.d: Total loss of reputation; public disgrace; dishonor; ignominy; indignity.
q: The afflicted queen would not yield, and said she would not . . . submit to such infamy.

senses.d: A quality which exposes to disgrace; extreme baseness or vileness; as, the infamy of an action.
That loss of character, or public disgrace, which a convict incurs, and by which he is at common law rendered incompetent as a witness.

Infamy.etym: [L. infamia, fr. infamis infamous; pref. in- not + fama fame: cf. F. infamie. See Fame.]

senses.d: A child in the first period of life, beginning at his birth; a young babe; sometimes, a child several years of age.
q: And tender cries of infants pierce the ear.

senses.d: A person who is not of full age, or who has not attained the age of legal capacity; a person under the age of twenty-one years; a minor.
Same as Infante.

Infant.etym: [L. infans; pref. in- not + fari to speak: cf. F. enfant, whence OE. enfaunt. See Fame, and cf. Infante, Infanta.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to infancy, or the first period of life; tender; not mature; as, infant strength.
Intended for young children; as, an infant school.
To bear or bring forth, as a child; hence, to produce, in general.
q: This worthy motto, “No bishop, no king,” is . . . infanted out of the same fears.

senses.d: Lower in place, rank, excellence, etc.; less important or valuable; subordinate; underneath; beneath.
q: A thousand inferior and particular propositions.
The body, or, as some love to call it, our inferior nature.
Whether they are equal or inferior to my other poems, an author is the most improper judge.

senses.d: Poor or mediocre; as, an inferior quality of goods.
Nearer the sun than the earth is; as, the inferior or interior planets; an inferior conjunction of Mercury or Venus.
Situated below some other organ; — said of a calyx when free from the ovary, and therefore below it, or of an ovary with an adherent and therefore inferior calyx.
Junior or subordinate in rank; as, an inferior officer.

Inferior.etym: [L., compar. of inferus that is below, underneath, the lower; akin to E. under: cf. F. inférieur. See Under.]

senses.d: A person lower in station, rank, intellect, etc., than another.
q: A great person gets more by obliging his inferior than by disdaining him.

senses.d: Not holding the faith; — applied esp. to one who does not believe in the inspiration of the Scriptures, and the supernatural origin of Christianity.
q: The infidel writer is a great enemy to society.

Infidel.etym: [L. infidelis; pref. in- not + fidelis faithful, fr. fides faith: cf. F. infidèle. See Fidelity.]

senses.d: One who does not believe in the prevailing religious faith; especially, one who does not believe in the divine origin and authority of Christianity; a Mohammedan; a heathen; a freethinker.

Infidel.syn: Infidel, Unbeliever, Freethinker, Deist, Atheist, Sceptic, Agnostic.

senses.d: Unlimited or boundless, in time or space; as, infinite duration or distance.
q: Whatever is finite, as finite, will admit of no comparative relation with infinity; for whatever is less than infinite is still infinitely distant from infinity; and lower than infinite distance the lowest or least can not sink.

senses.d: Without limit in power, capacity, knowledge, or excellence; boundless; immeasurably or inconceivably great; perfect; as, the infinite wisdom and goodness of God; — opposed to finite.
q: Great is our Lord, and of great power; his understanding is infinite.
O God, how infinite thou art!

senses.d: Indefinitely large or extensive; great; vast; immense; gigantic; prodigious.
q: Infinite riches in a little room.
Which infinite calamity shall cause To human life.

senses.d: Greater than any assignable quantity of the same kind; — said of certain quantities.

Capable of endless repetition; — said of certain forms of the canon, called also perpetual fugues, so constructed that their ends lead to their beginnings, and the performance may be incessantly repeated.

Infinite.syn: Boundless; immeasurable; illimitable; interminable; limitless; unlimited; endless; eternal.
Infinite.etym: [L. infinitus: cf. F. infini. See In- not, and Finite.]

senses.d: That which is infinite; boundless space or duration; infinity; boundlessness.
q: Not till the weight is heaved from off the air, and the thunders roll down the horizon, will the serene light of God flow upon us, and the blue infinite embrace us again.

senses.d: An infinite quantity or magnitude.
An infinity; an incalculable or very great number.
q: Glittering chains, embroidered richly o'er With infinite of pearls and finest gold.

senses.d: The Infinite Being; God; the Almighty.
The state of being infirm; feebleness; an imperfection or weakness; esp., an unsound, unhealthy, or debilitated state; a disease; a malady; as, infirmity of body or mind.
q: 'T is the infirmity of his age.

senses.d: A personal frailty or failing; foible; eccentricity; a weakness or defect.
q: Will you be cured of your infirmity ?
A friend should bear his friend's infirmities.
The house has also its infirmities.

Infirmity.syn: Debility; imbecility; weakness; feebleness; failing; foible; defect; disease; malady. See Debility.
Infirmity.etym: [L. infirmitas : cf. F. infirmite. See Infirm, a.]

senses.d: To set on fire; to kindle; to cause to burn, flame, or glow.
q: We should have made retreat By light of the inflamed fleet.

senses.d: Fig.: To kindle or intensify, as passion or appetite; to excite to an excessive or unnatural action or heat; as, to inflame desire.
q: Though more, it seems, Inflamed with lust than rage.
But, O inflame and fire our hearts.

senses.d: To provoke to anger or rage; to exasperate; to irritate; to incense; to enrage.
q: It will inflame you; it will make you mad.

senses.d: To put in a state of inflammation; to produce morbid heat, congestion, or swelling, of; as, to inflame the eyes by overwork.
To exaggerate; to enlarge upon.
q: A friend exaggerates a man's virtues, an enemy inflames his crimes.

Inflame.syn: To provoke; fire; kindle; irritate; exasperate; incense; enrage; anger; excite; arouse.
Inflame.etym: [OE. enflamen, OF. enflamer, F. enflammer, L. inflammare, inflammatum; pref. in- in + flammare to flame, fr. flamma flame. See Flame.]

senses.d: To grow morbidly hot, congested, or painful; to become angry or incensed.
The act of inflaming, kindling, or setting on fire; also, the state of being inflamed.

A morbid condition of any part of the body, consisting in congestion of the blood vessels, with obstruction of the blood current, and growth of morbid tissue. It is manifested outwardly by redness and swelling, attended with heat and pain.
Violent excitement; heat; passion; animosity; turbulence; as, an inflammation of the mind, of the body politic, or of parties.

Inflammation.etym: [L. inflammatio: cf. F. inflammation. See Inflame.]

senses.d: To give, cause, or produce by striking, or as if by striking; to apply forcibly; to lay or impose; to send; to cause to bear, feel, or suffer; as, to inflict blows; to inflict a wound with a dagger; to inflict severe pain by ingratitude; to inflict punishment on an offender; to inflict the penalty of death on a criminal.
q: What heart could wish, what hand inflict, this dire disgrace?
The persecution and the pain That man inflicts on all inferior kinds.

Inflict.etym: [L. inflictus, p. p. of infligere to strike on, to inflict; pref. in- in, on + fligere to strike. Cf. Flail.]

senses.d: A flowing in or upon; influx.
q: God hath his influence into the very essence of all things.

senses.d: Hence, in general, the bringing about of an effect, physical or moral, by a gradual process; controlling power quietly exerted; agency, force, or tendency of any kind which affects, modifies, or sways; as, the influence which the sun exerts on animal and vegetable life; the influence of education on the mind; the influence, according to astrologers, of the stars over affairs.
q: Astrologers call the evil influences of the stars, evil aspects.
Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?
She said : “Ah, dearest lord! what evil star On you hath frown'd, and poured, his influence bad?”

senses.d: Power or authority arising from elevated station, excelence of character or intellect, wealth, etc.; reputation; acknowledged ascendency; as, he is a man of influence in the community.
q: Such influence hath your excellency.

senses.d: Induction.

Influence.syn: Control; persuasion; ascendency; sway; power; authority; supremacy; mastery; management; restraint; character; reputation; prestige.
Influence.etym: [F. influence, fr. L. influens, -entis, p. pr. See Influent, and cf. Influenza.]

senses.d: To control or move by power, physical or moral; to affect by gentle action; to exert an influence upon; to modify, bias, or sway; to move; to persuade; to induce.
q: These experiments succeed after the same manner in vacuo as in the open air, and therefore are not influenced by the weight or pressure of the atmosphere.
This standing revelation . . . is sufficient to influence their faith and practice, if they attend.
The principle which influenced their obedience has lost its efficacy.

senses.d: To wrap up or cover with folds; to envelop; to inwrap; to inclose; to involve.
q: Gilded tombs do worms infold.
Infold his limbs in bands.

senses.d: To clasp with the arms; to embrace.
q: Noble Banquo, . . . let me infold thee, And hold thee to my heart.

senses.d: Without regular form; shapeless; ugly; deformed.

Inform.etym: [L. informis; pref. in- not + forma form, shape: cf. F. informe]

senses.d: To give form or share to; to give vital or organizing power to; to give life to; to imbue and actuate with vitality; to animate; to mold; to figure; to fashion.
q: Let others better mold the running mass Of metals, and inform the breathing brass.
Breath informs this fleeting frame.
Breathes in our soul, informs our mortal part.

senses.d: To communicate knowledge to; to make known to; to acquaint; to advise; to instruct; to tell; to notify; to enlighten; — usually followed by of.
q: For he would learn their business secretly, And then inform his master hastily.
I am informed thoroughly of the cause.

senses.d: To communicate a knowledge of facts to, by way of accusation; to warn against anybody.
q: Tertullus . . . informed the governor against Paul.

Inform.syn: To acquaint; apprise; tell; teach; instruct; enlighten; animate; fashion.
Inform.etym: [OE. enformen, OF. enformer, F. informer. L. informare; pref. in- in + formare to form, share, fr. forma form. See Form.]

senses.d: To take form; to become visible or manifest; to appear.
q: It is the bloody business which informs Thus to mine eyes.

senses.d: To give intelligence or information; to tell.
q: He might either teach in the same manner, or inform how he had been taught.

senses.d: Unformed or ill-formed; deformed; shapeless.
The act or business of gathering or collecting anything; especially, the gathering of the fruits of the earth; harvest.
q: Thou shalt keep . . . the feast of ingathering.

senses.d: To live or dwell in; to occupy, as a place of settled residence; as, wild beasts inhabit the forest; men inhabit cities and houses.
q: The high and lofty One, that inhabiteth eternity.
O, who would inhabit This bleak world alone?

Inhabit.etym: [OE. enhabiten, OF. enhabiter, L. inhabitare; pref. in- in + habitare to dwell. See Habit.]

senses.d: To have residence in a place; to dwell; to live; to abide.
q: They say wild beasts inhabit here.

senses.d: One who dwells or resides permanently in a place, as distinguished from a transient lodger or visitor; as, an inhabitant of a house, a town, a city, county, or state.
q: In this place, they report that they saw inhabitants which were very fair and fat people.

senses.d: One who has a legal settlement in a town, city, or parish; a permanent resident.
Uninhabited.
An inhabitant.

To take by descent from an ancestor; to take by inheritance; to take as heir on the death of an ancestor or other person to whose estate one succeeds; to receive as a right or title descendible by law from an ancestor at his decease; as, the heir inherits the land or real estate of his father; the eldest son of a nobleman inherits his father's title; the eldest son of a king inherits the crown.
To receive or take by birth; to have by nature; to derive or acquire from ancestors, as mental or physical qualities; as, he inherits a strong constitution, a tendency to disease, etc.
q: Prince Harry is valiant; for the cold blood he did naturally inherit of his father he hath . . . manured . . . with good store of fertile sherris.

senses.d: To come into possession of; to possess; to own; to enjoy as a possession.
q: But the meek shall inherit the earth.
To bury so much gold under a tree, And never after to inherit it.

senses.d: To put in possession of.

Inherit.etym: [OE. enheriten to inherit, to give a heritage to, OF. enheriter to appoint as an heir, L. inhereditare; pref. in- in + hereditare to inherit, fr. heres heir. See Heir.]

senses.d: To take or hold a possession, property, estate, or rights by inheritance.
q: Thou shalt not inherit our father's house.

senses.d: The act or state of inheriting; as, the inheritance of an estate; the inheritance of mental or physical qualities.
That which is or may be inherited; that which is derived by an heir from an ancestor or other person; a heritage; a possession which passes by descent.
q: When the man dies, let the inheritance Descend unto the daughter.

senses.d: A permanent or valuable possession or blessing, esp. one received by gift or without purchase; a benefaction.
q: To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away.

senses.d: Possession; ownership; acquisition.
q: To you th' inheritance belongs by right Of brother's praise; to you eke 'longs his love.

senses.d: Transmission and reception by animal or plant generation.

A perpetual or continuing right which a man and his heirs have to an estate; an estate which a man has by descent as heir to another, or which he may transmit to another as his heir; an estate derived from an ancestor to an heir in course of law.
q: Men are not proprietors of what they have, merely for themselves; their children have a title to part of it which comes to be wholly theirs when death has put an end to their parents' use of it; and this we call inheritance.

senses.d: One who inherits; an heir.
q: Born inheritors of the dignity.

senses.d: Absence of, or deviation from, just dealing; want of rectitude or uprightness; gross injustice; unrighteousness; wickedness; as, the iniquity of bribery; the iniquity of an unjust judge.
q: Till the world from his perfection fell Into all filth and foul iniquity.

senses.d: An iniquitous act or thing; a deed of injustice or unrighteousness; a sin; a crime.
q: Your iniquities have separated between you and your God.

senses.d: A character or personification in the old English moralities, or moral dramas, having the name sometimes of one vice and sometimes of another. See Vice.
q: Acts old Iniquity, and in the fit Of miming gets the opinion of a wit.

Iniquity.etym: [OE. iniquitee, F. iniquité, L. iniquitas, inequality, unfairness, injustice. See Iniquous.]

senses.d: To do harm to; to impair the excellence and value of; to hurt; to damage; — used in a variety of senses; as: (a) To hurt or wound, as the person; to impair soundness, as of health. (b) To damage or lessen the value of, as goods or estate. (c) To slander, tarnish, or impair, as reputation or character. (d) To impair or diminish, as happiness or virtue. (e) To give pain to, as the sensibilities or the feelings; to grieve; to annoy. (f) To impair, as the intellect or mind.
q: When have I injured thee? when done thee wrong?

Injure.syn: To damage; mar; spoil; harm; sully; wrong; maltreat; abuse; insult; affront; dishonor.
Injure.etym: [L. injuriari, fr. injuria injury, perh. through F. injurier to insult, in OF. also, to injure; or perhaps fr. E. injury, or F. injure injury. See Injury.]

senses.d: Not just; wrongful; iniquitous; culpable.
q: Till the injurious Roman did extort This tribute from us, we were free.

senses.d: Causing injury or harm; hurtful; harmful; detrimental; mischievous; as, acts injurious to health, credit, reputation, property, etc.
q: Without being injurious to the memory of our English Pindar.

Injurious.syn: Harmful; hurtful; pernicious; mischievous; baneful; deleterious; noxious; ruinous; detrimental.
Injurious.etym: [L. injuriousus, injurius; cf. F. injurieux. See Injury.]

senses.d: Want of justice and equity; violation of the rights of another or others; iniquity; wrong; unfairness; imposition.
q: If this people resembled Nero in their extravagance, much more did they resemble and even exceed him in cruelty and injustice.

senses.d: An unjust act or deed; a sin; a crime; a wrong.
q: Cunning men can be guilty of a thousand injustices without being discovered, or at least without being punished.

Injustice.etym: [F. injustice, L. injustitia. See In- not, and Justice, and cf. Unjust.]

senses.d: The step, or socket, in which the lower end of a millstone spindle runs.
A fluid, or a viscous material or preparation of various kinds (commonly black or colored), used in writing or printing.
q: Make there a prick with ink.
Deformed monsters, foul and black as ink.

senses.d: A pigment. See India ink, under India.

Ink.etym: [OE. enke, inke, OF. enque, F. encre, L. encaustum the purple red ink with which the Roman emperors signed their edicts, Gr. �, fr. � burnt in, encaustic, fr. � to burn in. See Encaustic, Caustic.]

senses.d: To put ink upon; to supply with ink; to blacken, color, or daub with ink.
A small bottle of horn or other material formerly used for holding ink; an inkstand; a portable case for writing materials.
q: From his pocket the notary drew his papers and inkhorn.

Inkhorn.etym: [Ink + horn; cf. F. cornet à encre, G. dintenhorn.]

senses.d: Learned; pedantic; affected.
A place of shelter; hence, dwelling; habitation; residence; abode.
q: Therefore with me ye may take up your inn For this same night.

senses.d: A house for the lodging and entertainment of travelers or wayfarers; a tavern; a public house; a hotel.
q: The miserable fare and miserable lodgment of a provincial inn.

senses.d: The town residence of a nobleman or distinguished person; as, Leicester Inn.
One of the colleges (societies or buildings) in London, for students of the law barristers; as, the Inns of Court; the Inns of Chancery; Serjeants' Inns.

Inn.etym: [AS. in, inn, house, chamber, inn, from AS. in in; akin to Icel. inni house. See In.]

senses.d: To take lodging; to lodge.
To house; to lodge.
q: When he had brought them into his city And inned them, everich at his degree.

senses.d: To get in; to in. See In, v. t.
In.
q: And eke in what array that they were inne.

senses.d: Further in; interior; internal; not outward; as, an inner chamber.
Of or pertaining to the spirit or its phenomena.
q: This attracts the soul, Governs the inner man, the nobler part.

senses.d: Not obvious or easily discovered; obscure.

Inner.etym: [AS. innera, a compar. fr. inne within, fr. in in. See In.]

senses.d: Farthest inward; most remote from the outward part; inmost; deepest within.

Innermost.etym: [A corruption of inmost due to influence of inner. See Inmost.]

senses.d: Innocence.
Not harmful; free from that which can injure; innoxious; innocuous; harmless; as, an innocent medicine or remedy.
q: The spear Sung innocent, and spent its force in air.

senses.d: Morally free from guilt; guiltless; not tainted with sin; pure; upright.
q: To offer up a weak, poor, innocent lamb.
I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood.
The aidless, innocent lady, his wished prey.

senses.d: Free from the guilt of a particular crime or offense; as, a man is innocent of the crime charged.
q: Innocent from the great transgression.

senses.d: Simple; artless; foolish.
Lawful; permitted; as, an innocent trade.
Not contraband; not subject to forfeiture; as, innocent goods carried to a belligerent nation.

Innocent.syn: Harmless; innoxious; innoffensive; guiltless; spotless; immaculate; pure; unblamable; blameless; faultless; guileless; upright.
Innocent.etym: [F. innocent, L. innocens, -entis; pref. in- not + nocens, p. pr. of nocere to harm, hurt. See Noxious.]

senses.d: An innocent person; one free from, or unacquainted with, guilt or sin.
An unsophisticated person; hence, a child; a simpleton; an idiot.
q: In Scotland a natural fool was called an innocent.

senses.d: Not capable of being counted, enumerated, or numbered, for multitude; countless; numberless; unnumbered, hence, indefinitely numerous; of great number.
q: Innumerable as the stars of night.

Innumerable.etym: [L. innumerabilis : cf. F. innumefable. See In- not, and Numerable.]

senses.d: Not limited to rules prescribed, or to usual bounds; irregular; excessive; immoderate; as, an inordinate love of the world.

Inordinate.etym: [L. inordinatus disordered. See In- not, and Ordinate.]

senses.d: The act of inquiring; inquiry; search; examination; inspection; investigation.
q: As I could learn through earnest inquisition.
Let not search and inquisition quail To bring again these foolish runaways.

senses.d: Judicial inquiry; official examination; inquest.
q: The justices in eyre had it formerly in charge to make inquisition concerning them by a jury of the county.

senses.d: A court or tribunal for the examination and punishment of heretics, fully established by Pope Gregory IX. in 1235. Its operations were chiefly confined to Spain, Portugal, and their dependencies, and a part of Italy.

Inquisition.etym: [L. inquisitio : cf. F. inquisition. See Inquire, and cf. Inquest.]

senses.d: To make inquisition concerning; to inquire into.
The act or process of inscribing.

That which is inscribed; something written or engraved; especially, a word or words written or engraved on a solid substance for preservation or public inspection; as, inscriptions on monuments, pillars, coins, medals, etc.
A line of division or intersection; as, the tendinous inscriptions, or intersections, of a muscle.
An address, consignment, or informal dedication, as of a book to a person, as a mark of respect or an invitation of patronage.

Inscription.etym: [L. inscriptio, fr. inscribere, inscriptum, to inscribe: cf. F. inscription. See Inscribe.]

senses.d: Within the sides of; in the interior; contained within; as, inside a house, book, bottle, etc.
Being within; included or inclosed in anything; contained; interior; internal; as, the inside passengers of a stagecoach; inside decoration.
q: Kissing with inside lip.

senses.d: Adapted to the interior.
The part within; interior or internal portion; content.
q: Looked he o' the inside of the paper?

senses.d: The inward parts; entrails; bowels; hence, that which is within; private thoughts and feelings.
q: Here's none but friends; we may speak Our insides freely.

senses.d: An inside passenger of a coach or carriage, as distinguished from one upon the outside.
q: So down thy hill, romantic Ashbourne, glides The Derby dilly, carrying three insides.

senses.d: So; to such a degree; in such wise; — followed by that or as, and formerly sometimes by both. Cf. Inasmuch.
q: Insomusch as that field is called . . . Aceldama.
Simonides was an excellent poet, insomuch that he made his fortune by it.

senses.d: The act of inspiring or breathing in; breath; specif. (Physiol.), the drawing of air into the lungs, accomplished in mammals by elevation of the chest walls and flattening of the diaphragm; — the opposite of expiration.

The act or power of exercising an elevating or stimulating influence upon the intellect or emotions; the result of such influence which quickens or stimulates; as, the inspiration of occasion, of art, etc.
q: Your father was ever virtuous, and holy men at their death have good inspirations.

senses.d: A supernatural divine influence on the prophets, apostles, or sacred writers, by which they were qualified to communicate moral or religious truth with authority; a supernatural influence which qualifies men to receive and communicate divine truth; also, the truth communicated.
q: All Scripture is given by inspiration of God.
The age which we now live in is not an age of inspiration and impulses.

senses.d: Pressing; urgent; importunate; earnest.
q: Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer.
I am beginning to be very instant for some sort of occupation.

senses.d: Closely pressing or impending in respect to time; not deferred; immediate; without delay.
q: Impending death is thine, and instant doom.

senses.d: Present; current.
q: The instant time is always the fittest time.

Instant.etym: [L. instans, -antis, p. pr. of instare to stand upon, to press upon; pref. in- in, on + stare to stand: cf. F. instant. See Stand.]

senses.d: Instantly.
q: Instant he flew with hospitable haste.

senses.d: A point in duration; a moment; a portion of time too short to be estimated; also, any particular moment.
q: There is scarce an instant between their flourishing and their not being.

senses.d: A day of the present or current month; as, the sixth instant; — an elliptical expression equivalent to the sixth of the month instant, i.e., the current month. See Instant, a., 3.

Instant.etym: [F. instant, fr. L. instans standing by, being near, present. See Instant, a.]

senses.d: Without the least delay or interval; at once; immediately.
With urgency or importunity; earnestly; pressingly.

Instantly.syn: Directly; immediately; at once. See Directly.

senses.d: In the place or room; — usually followed by of.
q: Let thistles grow of wheat.
Absalom made Amasa captain of the host instead of Joab.

senses.d: Equivalent; equal to; — usually with of.
q: This very consideration to a wise man is instead of a thousand arguments, to satisfy him, that in those times no such thing was believed.

senses.d: Arranged; furnished; provided.
Instructed; taught; enlightened.

Instruct.etym: [L. instructus, p. p. of instruere to furnish, provide, construct, instruct; pref. in- in, on + struere. See Structure.]

senses.d: To put in order; to form; to prepare.
q: They speak to the merits of a cause, after the proctor has prepared and instructed the same for a hearing.

senses.d: To form by communication of knowledge; to inform the mind of; to impart knowledge or information to; to enlighten; to teach; to discipline.
q: Schoolmasters will I keep within my house, Fit to instruct her youth.

senses.d: To furnish with directions; to advise; to direct; to command; as, the judge instructs the jury.
q: She, being before instructed of her mother, said, Give me here John Baptist's head in a charger.
Take her in; instruct her what she has to do.

Instruct.syn: To teach; educate; inform; train; discipline; indoctrinate; direct; enjoin.

senses.d: The act of instructing, teaching, or furnishing with knowledge; information.
That which instructs, or with which one is instructed; the intelligence or information imparted

Instruction.syn: Education; teaching; indoctrination; information; advice; counsel. See Education.

senses.d: One who instructs; one who imparts knowledge to another; a teacher.
That by means of which any work is performed, or result is effected; a tool; a utensil; an implement; as, the instruments of a mechanic; astronomical instruments.
q: All the lofty instruments of war.

senses.d: A contrivance or implement, by which musical sounds are produced; as, a musical instrument.
q: Praise him with stringed instruments and organs.
But signs when songs and instruments he hears.

senses.d: A writing, as the means of giving formal expression to some act; a writing expressive of some act, contract, process, as a deed, contract, writ, etc.
One who, or that which, is made a means, or is caused to serve a purpose; a medium, means, or agent.
q: Or useful serving man and instrument, To any sovereign state.
The bold are but the instruments of the wise.

Instrument.syn: Tool; implement; utensil; machine; apparatus; channel; agent.

senses.d: To perform upon an instrument; to prepare for an instrument; as, a sonata instrumented for orchestra.
A rising against civil or political authority, or the established government; open and active opposition to the execution of law in a city or state.
q: It is found that this city of old time hath made insurrection against kings, and that rebellion and sedition have been made therein.

senses.d: A rising in mass to oppose an enemy.
q: I say again, In soothing them, we nourish 'gainst our senate The cockle of rebellion, insolence, sedition.
Insurrections of base people are commonly more furious in their beginnings.
He was greatly strengthened, and the enemy as much enfeebled, by daily revolts.
Though of their names in heavenly records now Be no memorial, blotted out and razed By their rebellion from the books of life.

Insurrection.etym: [L. insurrectio, fr. insurgere, insurrectum: cf. F. insurrection. See Insurgent.]

senses.d: The state or quality of being entire or complete; wholeness; entireness; unbroken state; as, the integrity of an empire or territory.

Moral soundness; honesty; freedom from corrupting influence or motive; — used especially with reference to the fulfillment of contracts, the discharge of agencies, trusts, and the like; uprightness; rectitude.
q: The moral grandeur of independent integrity is the sublimest thing in nature.
Their sober zeal, integrity, and worth.

senses.d: Unimpaired, unadulterated, or genuine state; entire correspondence with an original condition; purity.
q: Language continued long in its purity and integrity.

Integrity.etym: [L. integritas: cf. F. intégrité. See Integer, and cf. Entirety.]

senses.d: The act or state of knowing; the exercise of the understanding.
The capacity to know or understand; readiness of comprehension; the intellect, as a gift or an endowment.
q: And dimmed with darkness their intelligence.

senses.d: Information communicated; news; notice; advice.
q: Intelligence is given where you are hid.

senses.d: Acquaintance; intercourse; familiarity.
q: He lived rather in a fair intelligence than any friendship with the favorites.

senses.d: Knowledge imparted or acquired, whether by study, research, or experience; general information.
q: I write as he that none intelligence Of meters hath, ne flowers of sentence.

senses.d: An intelligent being or spirit; — generally applied to pure spirits; as, a created intelligence.
q: The great Intelligences fair That range above our mortal state, In circle round the blessed gate, Received and gave him welcome there.

Intelligence.syn: Understanding; intellect; instruction; advice; notice; notification; news; information; report.
Intelligence.etym: [F. intelligence, L. intelligentia, intellegentia. See Intelligent.]

senses.d: To stretch; to extend; to distend.
q: By this the lungs are intended or remitted.

senses.d: To strain; to make tense.
q: When a bow is successively intended and remedied.

senses.d: To intensify; to strengthen.
q: Magnetism may be intended and remitted.

senses.d: To apply with energy.
q: Let him intend his mind, without respite, without rest, in one direction.

senses.d: To bend or turn; to direct, as one's course or journey.
To fix the mind on; to attend to; to take care of; to superintend; to regard.
q: Having no children, she did, with singular care and tenderness, intend the education of Philip.
My soul, not being able to intend two things at once, abated of its fervency in praying.

senses.d: To fix the mind upon (something to be accomplished); to be intent upon; to mean; to design; to plan; to purpose; — often followed by an infinitely with to, or a dependent clause with that; as, he intends to go; he intends that she shall remain.
q: They intended evil against thee.
To-morrow he intends To hunt the boar with certain of his friends.

senses.d: To design mechanically or artistically; to fashion; to mold.
q: Modesty was made When she was first intended.

senses.d: To pretend; to counterfeit; to simulate.
q: Intend a kind of zeal both to the prince and Claudio.

Intend.syn: To purpose; mean; design; plan; conceive; contemplate.
Intend.etym: [OE. entenden to be attentive, F. entendre, fr. L. intendre, intentum, and intensum, to intend, attend, stretch out, extend; pref. in- in + tendere to stretch, stretch out. See Tend.]

senses.d: Made tense; stretched out; extended; forcible; violent.
Purposed; designed; as, intended harm or help.
q: They drew a curse from an intended good.

senses.d: Betrothed; affianced; as, an intended husband.
One with whom marriage is designed; one who is betrothed; an affianced lover.
q: If it were not that I might appear to disparage his intended, . . . I would add that to me she seems to be throwing herself away.

senses.d: Closely directed; strictly attentive; bent; — said of the mind, thoughts, etc.; as, a mind intent on self-improvement.
Having the mind closely directed to or bent on an object; sedulous; eager in pursuit of an object; — formerly with to, but now with on; as, intent on business or pleasure.
q: Be intent and solicitous to take up the meaning of the speaker.

Intent.etym: [L. intentus, p. p. of intendere. See Intend, and cf. Intense.]

senses.d: The act of turning the mind toward an object; hence, a design; a purpose; intention; meaning; drift; aim.
q: Be thy intents wicked or charitable.
The principal intent of Scripture is to deliver the laws of duties supernatural.

Intent.syn: Design; purpose; intention; meaning; purport; view; drift; object; end; aim; plan.
Intent.etym: [OE. entent, entente, attention, purpose, OF. entente, F. entente understanding, meaning; a participial noun, fr. F. & OF. entendre. See Intend.]

senses.d: The act of interceding; mediation; interposition between parties at variance, with a view to reconcilation; prayer, petition, or entreaty in favor of, or (less often) against, another or others.
q: But the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which can not be uttered.

Intercession.etym: [L. intercessio an intervention, a becoming surety: cf. F. intercession. See Intercede.]

senses.d: One who goes between, or intercedes; a mediator. (a) One who interposes between parties at variance, with a view to reconcile them. (b) One who pleads in behalf of another.
A bishop, who, during a vacancy of the see, administers the bishopric till a successor is installed.
To meddle with the affairs of others; to meddle officiously; to interpose or interfere improperly; to mix or meddle with.
q: The practice of Spain hath been, by war and by conditions of treaty, to intermeddle with foreign states.

Intermeddle.etym: [OE. entremedlen, entermellen, to mix together, OF. entremedler, entremeller, entremesler, F. entremêler. See Inter-, and Meddle.]

senses.d: To intermix; to mingle.
q: Many other adventures are intermeddled.

senses.d: The act or the state of intermitting; the state of being neglected or disused; disuse; discontinuance.
Cessation for a time; an intervening period of time; an interval; a temporary pause; as, to labor without intermission; an intermission of ten minutes.
q: Rest or intermission none I find.

senses.d: The temporary cessation or subsidence of a fever; the space of time between the paroxysms of a disease. Intermission is an entire cessation, as distinguished from remission, or abatement of fever.
Intervention; interposition.

Intermission.syn: Cessation; interruption; interval; pause; stop; rest; suspension. See Cessation.
Intermission.etym: [L. intermissio: cf. F. intermission. See Intermit.]

senses.d: To explain or tell the meaning of; to expound; to translate orally into intelligible or familiar language or terms; to decipher; to define; — applied esp. to language, but also to dreams, signs, conduct, mysteries, etc.; as, to interpret the Hebrew language to an Englishman; to interpret an Indian speech.
q: Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us.
And Pharaoh told them his dreams; but there was none that could interpret them unto Pharaoh.

senses.d: To apprehend and represent by means of art; to show by illustrative representation; as, an actor interprets the character of Hamlet; a musician interprets a sonata; an artist interprets a landscape.

Interpret.syn: To translate; explain; solve; render; expound; elucidate; decipher; unfold; unravel.
Interpret.etym: [F. interprêter, L. interpretari, p. p. interpretatus, fr. interpres interpeter, agent, negotiator; inter between + (prob.) the root of pretium price. See Price.]

senses.d: To act as an interpreter.
The act of interpreting; explanation of what is obscure; translation; version; construction; as, the interpretation of a foreign language, of a dream, or of an enigma.
q: Look how we can, or sad or merrily, Interpretation will misquote our looks.

senses.d: The sense given by an interpreter; exposition or explanation given; meaning; as, commentators give various interpretations of the same passage of Scripture.
The power or explaining.
An artist's way of expressing his thought or embodying his conception of nature.
The act or process of applying general principles or formulæ to the explanation of the results obtained in special cases.

Interpretation.syn: Explanation; solution; translation; version; sense; exposition; rendering; definition.
