senses.d: One who or that which interprets, explains, or expounds; a translator; especially, a person who translates orally between two parties.
q: We think most men's actions to be the interpreters of their thoughts.

senses.d: To the inside of; within. It is used in a variety of applications.

Expressing entrance, or a passing from the outside of a thing to its interior parts; — following verbs expressing motion; as, come into the house; go into the church; one stream falls or runs into another; water enters into the fine vessels of plants.
Expressing penetration beyond the outside or surface, or access to the inside, or contents; as, to look into a letter or book; to look into an apartment.
Indicating insertion; as, to infuse more spirit or animation into a composition.
Denoting inclusion; as, put these ideas into other words.

Indicating the passing of a thing from one form, condition, or state to another; as, compound substances may be resolved into others which are more simple; ice is convertible into water, and water into vapor; men are more easily drawn than forced into compliance; we may reduce many distinct substances into one mass; men are led by evidence into belief of truth, and are often enticed into the commission of crimes; she burst into tears; children are sometimes frightened into fits; all persons are liable to be seduced into error and folly.
To thrust one's self in; to come or go in without invitation, permission, or welcome; to encroach; to trespass; as, to intrude on families at unseasonable hours; to intrude on the lands of another.
q: Thy wit wants edge And manners, to intrude where I am graced.
Some thoughts rise and intrude upon us, while we shun them; others fly from us, when we would hold them.

Intrude.etym: [L. intrudere, intrusum; pref. in- in + trudere to thrust, akin to E. threat. See Threat.]

senses.d: To thrust or force (something) in or upon; especially, to force (one's self) in without leave or welcome; as, to intrude one's presence into a conference; to intrude one's opinions upon another.
To enter by force; to invade.
q: Why should the worm intrude the maiden bud?

senses.d: The cause to enter or force a way, as into the crevices of rocks.

Intrude.syn: To obtrude; encroach; infringe; intrench; trespass. See Obtrude.

senses.d: To go into or upon; to pass within the confines of; to enter; — used of forcible or rude ingress.
q: Which becomes a body, and doth then invade The state of life, out of the grisly shade.

senses.d: To enter with hostile intentions; to enter with a view to conquest or plunder; to make an irruption into; to attack; as, the Romans invaded Great Britain.
q: Such an enemy Is risen to invade us.

senses.d: To attack; to infringe; to encroach on; to violate; as, the king invaded the rights of the people.
To grow or spread over; to affect injuriously and progressively; as, gangrene invades healthy tissue.

Invade.syn: To attack; assail; encroach upon. See Attack.
Invade.etym: [L. invadere, invasum; pref. in- in + vadere to go, akin to E. wade: cf. OF. invader, F. envahir. See Wade.]

senses.d: To make an invasion.
The act of invading; the act of encroaching upon the rights or possessions of another; encroachment; trespass.
A warlike or hostile entrance into the possessions or domains of another; the incursion of an army for conquest or plunder.
The incoming or first attack of anything hurtful or pernicious; as, the invasion of a disease.

Invasion.etym: [L. invasio: cf. F. invasion. See Invade.]

senses.d: To come or light upon; to meet; to find.
q: And vowed never to return again, Till him alive or dead she did invent.

senses.d: To discover, as by study or inquiry; to find out; to devise; to contrive or produce for the first time; — applied commonly to the discovery of some serviceable mode, instrument, or machine.
q: Thus first Necessity invented stools.

senses.d: To frame by the imagination; to fabricate mentally; to forge; — in a good or a bad sense; as, to invent the machinery of a poem; to invent a falsehood.
q: Whate'er his cruel malice could invent.
He had invented some circumstances, and put the worst possible construction on others.

Invent.syn: To discover; contrive; devise; frame; design; fabricate; concoct; elaborate. See Discover.
Invent.etym: [L. inventus, p. p. of invenire to come upon, to find, invent; pref. in- in + venire to come, akin to E. come: cf. F. inventer. See Come.]

senses.d: The act of finding out or inventing; contrivance or construction of that which has not before existed; as, the invention of logarithms; the invention of the art of printing.
q: As the search of it is the duty, so the invention will be the happiness of man.

senses.d: That which is invented; an original contrivance or construction; a device; as, this fable was the invention of Esop; that falsehood was her own invention.
q: We entered by the drawbridge, which has an invention to let one fall if not premonished.

senses.d: Thought; idea.
A fabrication to deceive; a fiction; a forgery; a falsehood.
q: Filling their hearers With strange invention.

senses.d: The faculty of inventing; imaginative faculty; skill or ingenuity in contriving anything new; as, a man of invention.
q: They lay no less than a want of invention to his charge; a capital crime, . . . for a poet is a maker.

senses.d: The exercise of the imagination in selecting and treating a theme, or more commonly in contriving the arrangement of a piece, or the method of presenting its parts.

Invention.etym: [L. inventio: cf. F. invention. See Invent.]

senses.d: One who invents or finds out something new; a contriver; especially, one who invents mechanical devices.
Incapable of being seen; not perceptible by vision; not visible.
q: To us invisible, or dimly seen In these thy lowest works.

Invisible.etym: [F. invisible, L. invisibilis. See In- not, and Visible.]

senses.d: An invisible person or thing; specifically, God, the Supreme Being.
A Rosicrucian; — so called because avoiding declaration of his craft.
One of those (as in the 16th century) who denied the visibility of the church.

To ask; to request; to bid; to summon; to ask to do some act, or go to some place; esp., to ask to an entertainment or visit; to request the company of; as, to invite to dinner, or a wedding, or an excursion.
q: So many guests invite as here are writ.
I invite his Grace of Castle Rackrent to reflect on this.

senses.d: To allure; to draw to; to tempt to come; to induce by pleasure or hope; to attract.
q: To inveigle and invite the unwary sense.
Shady groves, that easy sleep invite.
There no delusive hope invites despair.

senses.d: To give occasion for; as, to invite criticism.

Invite.syn: To solicit; bid; call; ask; summon; allure; attract; entice; persuade.
Invite.etym: [L. invitare: cf. F. inviter. See Vie.]

senses.d: To give invitation.
Being or placed within; inner; interior; — opposed to outward.
Seated in the mind, heart, spirit, or soul.
Intimate; domestic; private.
q: All my inward friends abhorred me.
He had had occasion, by one very inward with him, to know in part the discourse of his life.

Inward.etym: [AS. inweard, inneweard, innanweard, fr. innan, inne, within (fr. in in; see In) + the suffix -weard, E. -ward.]

senses.d: That which is inward or within; especially, in the plural, the inner parts or organs of the body; the viscera.
q: Then sacrificing, laid the inwards and their fat.

senses.d: The mental faculties; — usually pl.
An intimate or familiar friend or acquaintance.
Toward the inside; toward the center or interior; as, to bend a thing inward.
Into, or toward, the mind or thoughts; inwardly; as, to turn the attention inward.
q: So much the rather, thou Celestial Light, Shine inward.

Inward.etym: [AS. inweard. The ending -s is prop. a genitive ending. See Inward, a., -wards.]

senses.d: In the inner parts; internally.
q: Let Benedick, like covered fire, Consume away in sighs, waste inwardly.

senses.d: Toward the center; inward; as, to curve inwardly.
In the heart or mind; mentally; privately; secretly; as, he inwardly repines.
Intimately; thoroughly.
q: I shall desire to know him more inwardly.

senses.d: The most common and most useful metallic element, being of almost universal occurrence, usually in the form of an oxide (as hematite, magnetite, etc.), or a hydrous oxide (as limonite, turgite, etc.). It is reduced on an enormous scale in three principal forms; viz., cast iron, steel, and wrought iron. Iron usually appears dark brown, from oxidation or impurity, but when pure, or on a fresh surface, is a gray or white metal. It is easily oxidized (rusted) by moisture, and is attacked by many corrosive agents. Symbol Fe (Latin Ferrum). Atomic weight 55.9. Specific gravity, pure iron, 7.86; cast iron, 7.1. In magnetic properties, it is superior to all other substances.
An instrument or utensil made of iron; — chiefly in composition; as, a flatiron, a smoothing iron, etc.
q: My young soldier, put up your iron.

senses.d: Fetters; chains; handcuffs; manacles.
q: Four of the sufferers were left to rot in irons.

senses.d: Strength; power; firmness; inflexibility; as, to rule with a rod of iron.

Iron.etym: [OE. iren, AS. īren, īsen, īsern; akin to D. ijzer, OS. īsarn, OHG. īsarn, īsan, G. eisen, Icel. īsarn, jārn, Sw. & Dan. jern, and perh. to E. ice; cf. Ir. iarann, W. haiarn, Armor. houarn.]

senses.d: Of, or made of iron; consisting of iron; as, an iron bar, dust.
Resembling iron in color; as, iron blackness.
Like iron in hardness, strength, impenetrability, power of endurance, insensibility, etc.;
Rude; hard; harsh; severe.
q: Iron years of wars and dangers.
Jove crushed the nations with an iron rod.

senses.d: Firm; robust; enduring; as, an iron constitution.
Inflexible; unrelenting; as, an iron will.
Not to be broken; holding or binding fast; tenacious.
To smooth with an instrument of iron; especially, to smooth, as cloth, with a heated flatiron; — sometimes used with out.
To shackle with irons; to fetter or handcuff.
To furnish or arm with iron; as, to iron a wagon.
An iron-headed club with a deep face, chiefly used in making approaches, lifting a ball over hazards, etc.
The third person singular of the substantive verb be, in the indicative mood, present tense; as, he is; he is a man. See Be.
q: For thy is I come, and eke Alain.
Aye is thou merry.
To-morrow is the new moon.

Is.etym: [AS. is; akin to G. & Goth. ist, L. est, Gr. �, Skr. asti. √9. Cf. Am, Entity, Essence, Absent.]

senses.d: A descendant of Ishmael (the son of Abraham and Hagar), of whom it was said, “His hand will be against every man, and every man's hand against him.”
One at enmity with society; a wanderer; a vagabond; an outcast.
A tract of land surrounded by water, and smaller than a continent. Cf. Continent.
Anything regarded as resembling an island; as, an island of ice.

Island.etym: [OE. iland, yland, AS. īgland, �gland, �glond; īg, �g, island + land, lond, land. AS. īg, �g, is akin to AS. eá water, river, OHG. �uwa, G. au meadow, Icel. ey island, Dan. & Sw. ö, Goth. ahwa a stream, water, L. aqua water. The s is due to confusion with isle. Cf. Ait, Eyot, Ewer, Aquatic.]

senses.d: To cause to become or to resemble an island; to make an island or islands of; to isle.
To furnish with an island or with islands; as, to island the deep.
An island.
q: Imperial rule of all the seagirt isles.

senses.d: A spot within another of a different color, as upon the wings of some insects.

Isle.etym: [OF. isle, F. île, L. insula; cf. Lith. sala. Cf. Insulate.]

senses.d: To cause to become an island, or like an island; to surround or encompass; to island.
q: Isled in sudden seas of light.

senses.d: A descendant of Israel, or Jacob; a Hebrew; a Jew.

Israelite.etym: [L. Israëlites, Gr. �, fr. �, �, Israel, Heb. Yisrā�l, i.e., champion of God; sārāh to fight + �l God.]

senses.d: The act of passing or flowing out; a moving out from any inclosed place; egress; as, the issue of water from a pipe, of blood from a wound, of air from a bellows, of people from a house.
The act of sending out, or causing to go forth; delivery; issuance; as, the issue of an order from a commanding officer; the issue of money from a treasury.
That which passes, flows, or is sent out; the whole quantity sent forth or emitted at one time; as, an issue of bank notes; the daily issue of a newspaper.
Progeny; a child or children; offspring. In law, sometimes, in a general sense, all persons descended from a common ancestor; all lineal descendants.
q: If the king Should without issue die.

senses.d: Produce of the earth, or profits of land, tenements, or other property; as, A conveyed to B all his right for a term of years, with all the issues, rents, and profits.
A discharge of flux, as of blood.
An artificial ulcer, usually made in the fleshy part of the arm or leg, to produce the secretion and discharge of pus for the relief of some affected part.
The final outcome or result; upshot; conclusion; event; hence, contest; test; trial.
q: Come forth to view The issue of the exploit.
While it is hot, I 'll put it to the issue.

senses.d: A point in debate or controversy on which the parties take affirmative and negative positions; a presentation of alternatives between which to choose or decide.

In pleading, a single material point of law or fact depending in the suit, which, being affirmed on the one side and denied on the other, is presented for determination. See General issue, under General, and Feigned issue, under Feigned.

Issue.etym: [OF. issue, eissue, F. issue, fr. OF. issir, eissir, to go out, L. exire; ex out of, from + ire to go, akin to Gr. ιἔναι, Skr. i, Goth. iddja went, used as prefect of gaggan to go. Cf. Ambition, Count a nobleman, Commence, Errant, Exit, Eyre, Initial, Yede went.]

senses.d: To pass or flow out; to run out, as from any inclosed place.
q: From it issued forced drops of blood.

senses.d: To go out; to rush out; to sally forth; as, troops issued from the town, and attacked the besiegers.
To proceed, as from a source; as, water issues from springs; light issues from the sun.
To proceed, as progeny; to be derived; to be descended; to spring.
q: Of thy sons that shall issue from thee.

senses.d: To extend; to pass or open; as, the path issues into the highway.
To be produced as an effect or result; to grow or accrue; to arise; to proceed; as, rents and profits issuing from land, tenements, or a capital stock.
To close; to end; to terminate; to turn out; as, we know not how the cause will issue.
In pleading, to come to a point in fact or law, on which the parties join issue.
To send out; to put into circulation; as, to issue notes from a bank.
To deliver for use; as, to issue provisions.
To send out officially; to deliver by authority; as, to issue an order; to issue a writ.
The neuter pronoun of the third person, corresponding to the masculine pronoun he and the feminine she, and having the same plural (they, their or theirs, them).
q: The day present hath ever inough to do with it owne grief.
Do, child, go to it grandam, child.
It knighthood shall do worse. It shall fright all it friends with borrowing letters.
The fruit tree yielding fruit after his (its) kind.

It.etym: [OE. it, hit, AS. hit; cf. D. het. √181. See He.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to Italy, or to its people or language.

Italian.etym: [Cf. F. italien, It. italiano. Cf. Italic.]

senses.d: A native or inhabitant of Italy.
The language used in Italy, or by the Italians.
To have an uneasy sensation in the skin, which inclines the person to scratch the part affected.
q: My mouth hath itched all this long day.

senses.d: To have a constant desire or teasing uneasiness; to long for; as, itching ears.

Itch.etym: [OE. icchen, ”icchen, AS. giccan; akin to D. jeuken, joken, G. jucken, OHG. jucchen.]

senses.d: An eruption of small, isolated, acuminated vesicles, produced by the entrance of a parasitic mite (the Sarcoptes scabei), and attended with itching. It is transmissible by contact.
Any itching eruption.
A sensation in the skin occasioned (or resembling that occasioned) by the itch eruption; — called also scabies, psora, etc.
A constant irritating desire.
q: An itch of being thought a divine king.

senses.d: Possessive form of the pronoun it. See It.
The neuter reciprocal pronoun of It; as, the thing is good in itself; it stands by itself.
q: Borrowing of foreigners, in itself, makes not the kingdom rich or poor.

senses.d: The hard, white, opaque, fine-grained substance constituting the tusks of the elephant. It is a variety of dentine, characterized by the minuteness and close arrangement of the tubes, as also by their double flexure. It is used in manufacturing articles of ornament or utility.
The tusks themselves of the elephant, etc.
Any carving executed in ivory.
Teeth; as, to show one's ivories.

Ivory.etym: [OE. ivori, F. ivoire, fr. L. eboreus made of ivory, fr. ebur, eboris, ivory, cf. Skr. ibha elephant. Cf. Eburnean.]
